problem: Visual navigation systems treat the environment as static and fail when unavoidable obstructions block the path; existing interactive-navigation RL methods rely on non-photorealistic simulators or vector inputs, lack memory in maze-like scenes and transfer poorly to real robots.
motivation: Real environments such as buildings contain movable obstacles, so an agent should decide whether pushing an obstacle is better than detouring. Sample-inefficient RL on high-res visuals and reactive policies without memory hinder deployment, motivating a self-supervised, hierarchical, map-based approach trained on photorealistic data.
key_idea: A hierarchical planner combining a global traversability-semantic grid map (A*) with a local RNN/VAE-based planner trained imperatively on a differentiable costmap derived from the simulator navigation mesh, enabling self-supervised interactive navigation with zero-shot sim-to-real transfer.
insight: Ablations show latent regularization (stochastic VAE), recurrent memory, and auxiliary objectives (predictive VAE, odometry) each improve generalization to unseen obstacles/textures. E.g. on House 2 the Deterministic variant drops SR from 0.96 to 0.62 and OnlyVAE to 0.70, while the minimal Baseline matches only in the non-interactive Forest and falls to 0.68 SR in the maze-like houses. Costmap-derived labels give consistency between global and local planning.
method: Perception (VAE): encodes depth with a residual CNN plus frozen DINOv2 RGB features into a [23,40,8] latent (7360 variables); decodes depth reconstruction and a pixel-wise traversability mask (free / movable / non-traversable).

Global mapping and planning: back-projects the traversability mask into a 2D grid map with weighted-average updates (observation count clipped to 100 so moving-obstacle artifacts decay), then runs A* with different penalties for movable and non-traversable cells; the closest point in line of sight becomes the subgoal.

Local planner: convolutional GRU takes the latent parameters and subgoal, maintains a belief state, and a Path-CNN predicts N waypoints; the GRU also predicts the next latent (predictive VAE) as a latent-dynamics side objective.
Auxiliary odometry head: predicts the pose change from consecutive hidden states as a second side objective.

Imperative self-supervised training: the path loss (obstacle cost sampled from a differentiable costmap built from the SPEAR navigation mesh, waypoint spacing, goal distance) plus traversability cross-entropy, with labels generated automatically from the costmap using obstacle mass/friction/inclination heuristics.
Robustification: GPU-vectorized ICL-NIUM depth-noise simulation (~500x speedup), RGB white noise, and injection of real SUN-RGBD depth images for sim-to-real.

setting.backbone: Custom VAE + convolutional GRU + Path-CNN with frozen DINOv2 ViT features (trained from scratch apart from DINOv2)
setting.training_data: Synthetic sequential data from Intel SPEAR simulator with domain randomization, mixed with real SUN-RGBD depth images; 10 epochs, AdamW
setting.action_space: predicted local waypoints (N waypoints to a subgoal) tracked by the robot; simulation agent moves straight between waypoints with in-place rotations
setting.privileged: none at test time (navigation mesh used only for training data/labels and for SPL computation; goal position given)

numbers_note: Metrics are printed as fractions (0.97), kept as printed; the benchmarks are the authors' own SPEAR scenes. Real-world results are qualitative only.
results: The proposed planner achieves SR 0.96-0.97 and SPL 0.74-0.78 across the three SPEAR scenes, and beats the minimal Baseline strongly in the interactive houses (SR 0.97 vs 0.68 on House 1, 0.96 vs 0.68 on House 2). It transfers zero-shot to an ANYmal D, distinguishing and pushing movable objects.
limitations: Sim-to-real transfer remains imperfect; movability reasoning is heuristic-based and relies on learned appearance cues
Evaluation is on only three custom simulated scenes, with no comparison to other published interactive-navigation methods and only qualitative real-world results
Simulation agent uses simplified straight-line motion and does not model precise physical interaction dynamics
compares_to: Baseline (Bansal et al. 2019 style direct waypoint prediction)
